questions.stem: Which three factors most often limit the rate of photosynthesis in a crop?

options.text: Temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Soil pH, wind speed and humidity
options.explanation: Those affect plants, but the taught trio is different.

options.text: Water depth, salinity and pressure
options.explanation: Aquatic conditions are not the crop factors here.

options.text: Potassium, phosphate and calcium levels
options.explanation: Those are mineral ions, not the photosynthesis limiters.

questions.stem: What happens to photosynthesis as temperature climbs past a certain point?

options.text: The plant switches to darkness chemistry
options.explanation: No such switch occurs.

options.text: The rate falls because the enzymes controlling the reaction denature
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The rate keeps climbing without limit
options.explanation: Denaturation reverses the trend.

options.text: The rate stays exactly the same
options.explanation: The curve turns downward past the optimum.

questions.stem: Why does raising carbon dioxide concentration speed up photosynthesis?

options.text: It gives the enzymes extra energy
options.explanation: Enzymes are not fuelled by carbon dioxide.

options.text: It replaces the need for light
options.explanation: Light remains a separate requirement.

options.text: Carbon dioxide is a raw material the reaction consumes
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Carbon dioxide warms the leaf directly
options.explanation: Any warming is separate from the raw-material role.

questions.stem: Light intensity on a crop is doubled, yet the rate barely moves. What does that reveal?

options.text: The light meter is broken
options.explanation: The plateau signals a different bottleneck.

options.text: The plant has stopped photosynthesising
options.explanation: The rate continues, just uncapped by light.

options.text: Extra light always poisons leaves
options.explanation: Light does not poison; scarcity elsewhere caps the rate.

options.text: Some other factor is now limiting the rate
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A glasshouse on a cold dull morning gets heaters and lamps switched on. Which input still caps the rate?

options.text: Whichever of temperature, light or carbon dioxide remains scarcest after the changes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Soil temperature alone from then on
options.explanation: Soil temperature is not one of the three.

options.text: Nothing can ever limit again
options.explanation: Some factor always sets the ceiling.

options.text: The growers' electricity supply
options.explanation: That is a cost issue, not a plant factor.

questions.stem: State the term for the factor in shortest supply that caps photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: The limiting factor is the scarcest input, and it sets the ceiling on the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Name the raw material gases that a glasshouse enriches to speed photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide is enriched in the glasshouse air so photosynthesis can proceed faster.

questions.stem: Explain why warming helps a cool crop only up to a point.
questions.modelAnswer: Enzymes drive photosynthesis, so moderate warming raises their activity, but past the optimum their working surfaces denature and the rate drops sharply.

questions.stem: A tomato grower already provides bright light and warm air. Recommend the next control to raise yield.
questions.modelAnswer: Enrich the air with carbon dioxide, because with light and temperature already high that is the factor most likely to be limiting photosynthesis.
